passages.title: The Language of the Hive
passages.subtitle: How honeybees share the location of food, and how scientists learned to read their messages

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has kept bees will have noticed a curious pattern. When a single forager finds a rich patch of flowers, it is rarely long before dozens of her nestmates arrive at exactly the same spot, even when it lies far from the hive and out of sight behind trees or buildings. Naturalists puzzled over this for centuries. Aristotle observed that on any one trip a bee tends to visit only a single kind of flower, but neither he nor the many observers who came after him could explain how knowledge of a distant food source spread through a colony. It was not until the twentieth century that the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch proposed an answer so unexpected that many of his fellow scientists found it hard to accept: bees were telling each other where to go by dancing.

Von Frisch began studying bees in the 1910s, and his early work had nothing to do with communication. He first set out to show that bees could see colour, which at the time was widely doubted, by training them to collect sugar water from a blue card placed among grey cards of varying shades. It was while running feeding experiments of this kind that he noticed something odd. After he refilled an empty feeding dish, the first bee to find it would return to the hive, and within minutes many new bees would appear. To find out what was happening inside, he built hives with glass walls and marked individual bees with small dots of paint so that he could follow their behaviour.

What he saw was a returning forager performing a rapid, repeated movement on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. In what came to be called the ‘waggle dance’, the bee runs forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point, first to the right and then to the left, before beginning the straight run again. The pattern can be repeated dozens of times, and the dancer is usually followed closely by other bees, which press their antennae against her body as she moves. Since the inside of a hive is almost completely dark, these followers cannot watch the dance in any ordinary sense; instead, they read it through touch, vibration and the faint air currents created by the dancer’s wings.

Over many years of patient observation, von Frisch worked out that the straight ‘waggle run’ contains two separate pieces of information. Its angle encodes direction. On the vertical comb, straight up represents the direction of the sun, so a bee running straight upwards is telling her audience to fly directly towards the sun, while a run angled 40 degrees to the right of vertical indicates a food source 40 degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of the waggle run, meanwhile, encodes distance: the longer the run lasts, the further away the food is. The precise relationship varies between colonies and between the different subspecies of honeybee, but as a rough guide, a waggle run lasting one second corresponds to a flight of about a kilometre. For food very close to the hive, von Frisch described a simpler ‘round dance’, which signals that food is nearby without indicating a direction. Researchers today tend to regard this not as a separate behaviour but as a version of the waggle dance in which the runs are extremely short.

One of the most remarkable features of the system is that the dance is adjusted as time passes. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a bee dancing for the same flower patch in the afternoon will point in a different direction from one dancing in the morning. Von Frisch found that experienced foragers compensate for this movement automatically, even when they have spent a long time inside the hive without seeing the sky. Bees also appear to judge distance not by the energy they use in flight but by the amount of visual movement they experience on the way. In later experiments, bees that flew through a narrow tunnel lined with a busy pattern danced as though they had travelled much further than they actually had.

Von Frisch published his conclusions in full in the 1940s, and in 1973 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with two other pioneers in the study of animal behaviour. Yet his theory was far from universally accepted. During the 1960s, the American biologist Adrian Wenner argued that recruited bees found food by following scent alone, and that the dance, however striking, carried no useful information. The debate continued for decades, partly because it was so difficult to prove what the followers were actually doing once they had left the hive.

Two developments finally settled the matter. In the early 1990s, a team of Danish and German researchers built a small robotic bee, which they placed in a hive and programmed to perform waggle dances. Living bees followed the robot and then searched in the locations it indicated, even though the robot carried no scent from any real flower. Then, in 2005, a British–German team attached tiny radar transponders to recruited bees and tracked their flights. The recruits flew almost directly towards the area indicated by the dance, and only then began to fly in loops, apparently searching for further clues such as scent before finding the exact source. Both sides of the old argument, it seemed, had been partly right: the dance provides a general map reference, and other senses guide the final approach.

Today, the waggle dance is regarded as one of the most sophisticated examples of symbolic communication in the animal kingdom, and it is also proving useful to humans. By filming dances and decoding them, researchers can map where the bees of a colony are feeding across the landscape, and at which times of year. Such ‘dance decoding’ studies have shown, for example, that colonies in some regions travel much further to find food in late summer than in spring, information that can help farmers and conservationists decide which plants to grow in order to support pollinators.

passages.title: The Box That Shrank the World
passages.subtitle: How a standard steel container transformed trade, ports and the global economy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, moving goods by sea was slow, expensive and labour-intensive. Cargo travelled as ‘break-bulk’: sacks of coffee, barrels of oil, crates of machinery and bales of cotton were loaded one by one into the hold of a ship, often by gangs of dockworkers using little more than hooks, ropes and their own muscles. A single vessel might carry many thousands of separate items, each of which had to be lifted, stacked and secured, and then unloaded and sorted again at the other end. It was not unusual for a cargo ship to spend as long tied up in port as it did at sea, and losses from breakage and theft were accepted as a routine cost of doing business.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The man most often credited with changing this was not a shipowner at all but a trucking entrepreneur from North Carolina named Malcolm McLean. Frustrated by the hours his drivers spent waiting at the docks while their loads were transferred to ships, McLean began to wonder whether it might be possible to lift the entire body of a truck trailer on board and leave the wheels behind. In April 1956, a converted wartime tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying 58 metal boxes on a specially built deck. When McLean later calculated the costs of the voyage, he found that loading cargo in this way had cost less than a twentieth of the conventional price.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: McLean was not the first person to put goods in boxes; railways and shipping lines had experimented with various kinds of containers since the nineteenth century. His innovation lay in seeing the container not as a piece of equipment but as the basis for an entirely new system. Ships, cranes, trucks and port terminals all had to be redesigned around the box, and McLean was willing to invest heavily, and to take enormous financial risks, in order to make this happen. Within a decade, his company was operating purpose-built container ships, and specialised cranes could transfer a box between ship and shore in a matter of minutes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The early years of containerisation, however, were marked by confusion. Different companies used containers of different lengths and heights, with incompatible fittings for lifting and locking them together, so that a box belonging to one shipping line often could not be handled by another line’s equipment. Only after lengthy and often bad-tempered negotiations during the 1960s did international bodies agree on a set of common standards, including the now-familiar lengths of 20 and 40 feet and a standard corner fitting that allowed any container to be lifted by any crane and locked onto any ship, train or truck. Capacity in the industry is still measured today in ‘TEU’, or twenty-foot equivalent units.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: One unexpected factor in the spread of the container was war. When the United States sent large numbers of troops to Vietnam in the mid-1960s, military supply lines were overwhelmed and ports in the region became badly congested. McLean’s company won a contract to carry military cargo by container, which dramatically reduced delays. Rather than sail back across the Pacific with empty ships, McLean looked for cargo to carry on the return journey and found it in Japan, which was then emerging as a major manufacturing economy. The container thus helped to open up the trade routes between Asia and North America that dominate world shipping today.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For the communities that had grown up around traditional ports, the consequences were often painful. Container terminals required vast areas of flat land for storing boxes, as well as good connections to roads and railways, and old city-centre docks, hemmed in by buildings, could rarely provide these. In city after city, activity shifted to new locations, sometimes many kilometres away: in New York, most traffic moved across the harbour to New Jersey, while in Britain, the small port of Felixstowe grew rapidly as the historic docks of London declined. Because a container terminal needed only a fraction of the labour of a break-bulk port, tens of thousands of dockworkers lost their jobs, often after bitter industrial disputes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Economists continue to debate how much of the growth in international trade since the 1960s can be attributed to the container, but few doubt that its influence has been enormous. By cutting transport costs and making delivery times more reliable, the box made it practical for manufacturers to source components from factories on the other side of the world and to assemble products wherever costs were lowest. The largest vessels afloat today can carry more than 24,000 TEU, and a container of clothing or electronics can travel from a factory in Asia to a shop in Europe for a cost that adds only a few cents to the price of each item. Yet the system’s efficiency also makes it vulnerable: when a single large ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days in 2021, the disruption to global supply chains was felt for months.

passages.title: The Puzzle of the Placebo
passages.subtitle: Why do inactive treatments sometimes make people feel better, and what should medicine do about it?

paragraphs.text: In modern medicine, the placebo has an awkward double identity. On the one hand, it is a tool: in a randomised controlled trial, patients who receive a new drug are compared with those who receive an inactive substitute, such as a sugar pill, so that researchers can tell whether the drug does anything beyond the effect of simply being treated. On the other hand, the placebo is a phenomenon in its own right, and a puzzling one. If a pill contains no active ingredient, why should anyone who takes it feel any better at all?

For much of the twentieth century, doctors were confident that placebos were powerful. The most influential statement of this view came in 1955, when the American anaesthetist Henry Beecher published a paper with the memorable title ‘The Powerful Placebo’. Having reviewed fifteen studies involving more than a thousand patients, Beecher concluded that around 35 per cent of people experienced satisfactory relief from placebos alone. The figure was repeated in textbooks for decades and helped to establish the idea that the mind could produce substantial physical improvements simply through belief.

Later researchers, however, found serious problems with Beecher’s reasoning. Most of the studies he relied on had no group of patients who received no treatment at all, so there was no way of knowing how many of them would have improved anyway. Many illnesses get better on their own, and symptoms that are at their worst when a patient first seeks help often become milder with time, a statistical effect known as regression to the mean. In 2001, the Danish researchers Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche analysed well over a hundred trials that had included both a placebo group and an untreated group. They found little evidence that placebos had powerful effects in general, though there were signs of modest benefits for outcomes that patients themselves reported, particularly pain.

Pain, indeed, is where the placebo response has been studied most closely, and where some of the clearest evidence of a biological mechanism has emerged. In a classic experiment in 1978, researchers in California gave placebos to patients recovering from dental surgery. Some patients reported less pain after the placebo, but when they were also given naloxone, a drug that blocks the action of the body’s natural painkillers, known as endorphins, the effect disappeared. The implication was that, at least in some cases, expecting relief can cause the brain to release its own pain-relieving chemicals. Since then, the Italian neuroscientist Fabrizio Benedetti and others have mapped many of the brain regions involved, showing that the placebo response is not imaginary but a real physiological event.

The strength of the response seems to depend heavily on context. Studies have found that two placebo pills tend to have a greater effect than one, that injections are generally more effective than pills, and that the colour of a tablet can affect how patients expect it to act. Even price appears to matter: in a 2008 study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, volunteers who were told that a painkiller cost $2.50 per pill reported greater relief from mild electric shocks than those told it had been discounted to ten cents, although both groups received the same inactive pill. The manner of the doctor also plays a role. A warm, attentive practitioner who expresses confidence in a treatment can amplify its effect, while a brisk and distant one may reduce it.

The same mechanisms can work in reverse. Patients who are warned that a treatment may cause side effects are more likely to report them, even when they have received only a placebo, a phenomenon known as the nocebo effect. In clinical trials of cholesterol-lowering drugs, for example, many participants who were given dummy pills reported muscle pain and abandoned the treatment. For doctors, this creates an uncomfortable dilemma: they have an ethical duty to inform patients about possible risks, yet good reason to believe that doing so may cause some of those very symptoms.

The ethical difficulties do not end there. For a doctor to prescribe a placebo in ordinary practice has traditionally meant deceiving the patient, which most medical codes now consider unacceptable. In 2010, however, a team led by Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard Medical School published a study that challenged the assumption that deception was necessary. Patients with irritable bowel syndrome were given pills that they were openly told contained no medicine, together with an explanation that placebos had been shown to produce improvement through mind–body processes. After three weeks, these patients reported significantly greater relief from their symptoms than a comparison group who received no pills at all. Similar ‘open-label’ studies have since been carried out on conditions ranging from back pain to fatigue, though most have been small, and critics point out that patients who agree to take part may be unusually receptive to the idea.

What, then, is a placebo? It is increasingly clear that the question has been framed in the wrong way. The sugar pill itself does nothing; what matters is everything that surrounds it: the ritual of treatment, the patient’s expectations, previous experience of medicines that worked, and the relationship with the person providing care. Seen in this light, the placebo effect is not a strange exception to the rules of medicine but a reminder that every treatment is delivered to a person as well as to a body. The challenge for medicine is to harness these effects honestly, without allowing them to become an excuse for treatments that have no genuine value of their own.
